maths_eduqas_f.4.5.summary: Systematic enumeration is the foundation of working out probabilities without missing any possible combinations. By learning to construct and interpret tables, grids, Venn diagrams, and tree diagrams, you can systematically list out every single outcome in an exhaustive sample space. Mastery of these four visual tools ensures full accuracy in counting outcomes for both single and combined events under the Eduqas Foundation specification.

core.p: Systematic listing means writing down every possible outcome in an organised way so that none are missed or repeated. In exam questions, you must show a clear method rather than guessing numbers.
bullets: Always use a logical pattern: alphabetical, numerical, or size order.
Check your total count against multiplication rules (e.g., 3 options times 4 options = 12 outcomes).
Understand that 'enumerate' literally means to count or list one by one.

callouts.p: An exhaustive list contains every single possible outcome without gaps.

core.h: 2. Using Tables for Two Independent Events
core.p: Tables provide a two-dimensional grid where rows represent one event and columns represent another. They are perfect for tracking the outcomes of two separate actions, like spinning two spinners or rolling two dice.
bullets: Place the outcomes of the first event along the top row.
Place the outcomes of the second event down the left-hand column.
Fill in the inner cells with combined outcomes, such as coordinate pairs or sums.

callouts.p: When listing combined outcomes in cells, keep the order consistent (e.g., always event 1 then event 2).

fig.cap: A 2D probability table showing all 6 combined outcomes for a letter spinner and a number spinner.

core.p: Possibility space grids are commonly used for games involving two dice or spinners where you calculate sums, products, or differences of the outcomes.
bullets: Draw a standard Cartesian grid with axes labelled with the possible scores.
Calculate the required mathematical operation (like addition for dice sums) inside every cell.
Count favourable outcomes directly from the grid cells.

callouts.p: Remember (1,2) and (2,1) are distinct outcomes when rolling two separate dice, even if the numbers are the same.

core.p: Venn diagrams use overlapping circles within a universal set rectangle to sort items into categories based on specific rules or attributes.
bullets: The rectangle represents the universal set (denoted by the Greek letter Xi, ξ).
Each circle represents a specific set or condition (e.g., multiples of 3).
The intersection (where circles overlap) contains items that satisfy both conditions simultaneously.

callouts.p: The universal set contains all the possible objects under consideration in a given problem.

fig.cap: A Venn diagram showing a universal set with two intersecting sets A and B.

core.p: When given a list of numbers or objects, sorting them into a Venn diagram requires checking each item against the criteria for each set in turn.
bullets: Always start by placing items that belong in the intersection (middle region) first.
Next, place items that belong in just one set, crossing them off your original list.
Finally, place any remaining items that fit neither set in the outside space inside the rectangle.

callouts.p: Sum up all the numbers placed in every region of the Venn diagram; their total must equal the total items in the original list.

core.p: Exam questions often ask you to shade specific regions or find probabilities based on given numbers in a completed Venn diagram.
bullets: A union (A U B) means everything inside circle A, circle B, and their overlap.
An intersection (A \u2229 B) means strictly the overlapping middle section.
A complement (A') means everything except circle A.

callouts.p: Remember 'Union' sounds like 'Unite' (everything together), while 'Intersection' is where roads cross (the overlap).

core.p: Tree diagrams map out sequential events that happen one after another. They consist of 'branches' representing the outcomes of each step.
bullets: Draw a starting node on the left.
Draw first-generation branches for the first event.
Draw second-generation branches from the end of each first branch for the second event.

callouts.p: A line segment on a tree diagram representing a specific outcome of an event.

fig.cap: A basic tree diagram structure showing two sequential events with two outcomes each.

core.p: At Foundation tier, tree diagrams are frequently used simply to list all possible combined outcomes by following every unique path from left to right.
bullets: Trace the top path from start to finish and write down the combined result.
Continue tracing every branch combination systematically.
Count the final endpoints to verify the total number of combined outcomes.

callouts.p: If event 1 has 3 outcomes and event 2 has 2 outcomes, your tree diagram must end with 3 \u00d7 2 = 6 final outcomes.

core.p: Choosing the correct visual tool makes solving probability and counting problems much faster and prevents mistakes.
bullets: Use tables/grids for two events with numerical or categorical outcomes.
Use Venn diagrams for classifying items that may share overlapping properties.
Use tree diagrams for events that happen in chronological sequence.

core.h: 10. Solving Exam Word Problems with Systematic Lists
core.p: Exam questions often present real-life scenarios like choosing outfits, meal deals, or travel routes, requiring you to list options systematically.
bullets: Break the problem down into sequential choices (e.g., starter, main, dessert).
Use a systematic tree diagram or systematic list to show all combinations.
Read the question carefully to see if order matters or if any restrictions apply.

callouts.p: Writing random guesses will lose marks; markers specifically look for a systematic method.

analogy.p: Imagine you are designing a set-menu where customers choose one starter and one main course. A systematic table or tree diagram acts like the kitchen order system, ensuring every single meal combination is accounted for without the chef getting confused or missing an item. Where the analogy breaks down is that mathematical sets can overlap and share elements (like a dish that is both spicy and vegetarian), whereas menu items are usually mutually exclusive categories.

terms.d: A method of writing out every possible outcome in a logical, rule-based order so none are missed.
The complete set of all possible outcomes of an experiment or trial.
A table that displays outcomes or frequencies for two categorical variables using rows and columns.
A visual grid showing all possible outcomes of a combined event.
A diagram using overlapping circles to show relationships between different sets of items.
The set containing all objects or elements under consideration, represented by \u03be.
The overlapping region of a Venn diagram containing items that belong to multiple sets at once.
The combined region of sets in a Venn diagram containing items belonging to either set or both.
Everything outside a given set, denoted by an apostrophe like A'.
A diagram with branches used to show outcomes of sequential events.
A point on a tree diagram where branches split into further possible outcomes.
A set of outcomes that includes every single possibility without omission.

mistakes.w: Writing combined outcomes in random, messy orders without a pattern.
mistakes.r: Always use a strict alphabetical, numerical, or logical sequence (e.g., (1,1), (1,2), (1,3)).

mistakes.w: Forgetting to include the outer region of a Venn diagram for items fitting no categories.
mistakes.r: Always check if any items from the master list do not fit inside the circles, and place them inside the universal rectangle outside the circles.

mistakes.w: Drawing tree diagrams with unequal numbers of branches where categories are identical.
mistakes.r: Ensure each set of branches accurately reflects the given options for that specific stage.

mistakes.w: Counting duplicate outcomes when rolling identical dice.
mistakes.r: Treat dice as distinct objects (e.g., Red die and Blue die) so (1,2) and (2,1) are counted separately.

mistakes.w: Confusing union and intersection on Venn diagrams.
mistakes.r: Union is all combined elements; intersection is strictly the overlapping middle section.

mistakes.w: Listing (A,B) and (B,A) as the same outcome in a two-way table.
mistakes.r: Respect the axis order; row-column coordinates represent ordered pairs.

mistakes.w: Leaving out labels on tree diagram branches or Venn diagram regions.
mistakes.r: Always fully label every set, region, and branch so the examiner can follow your work.

exam.q: A sandwich shop offers a choice of 3 breads (White, Brown, Wrap) and 2 fillings (Cheese, Ham). Complete a systematic list to show all possible single-filling sandwich combinations.
exam.tip: Pair every single bread option with every single filling systematically.

exam.q: A fair six-sided die and a fair coin are tossed together. Complete a sample space grid to show all 12 possible outcomes.
model: Grid axes correctly labelled 1 to 6 and Head/Tail
All 12 coordinate pairs correctly filled in cells
exam.tip: Use rows for the coin and columns for the die numbers.

exam.q: 50 students are asked if they study History (H) or Geography (G). 20 study History only, 15 study Geography only, 5 study both. Complete the Venn diagram for this information.
model: 15 placed in the G-only region and 10 outside in \u03be
exam.tip: Always fill in the intersection first before doing subtraction for single-set regions.

exam.q: Shade the region representing A \u2229 B' on a two-circle Venn diagram.
model: Circle A shaded entirely except the overlapping region with B
exam.tip: B' means outside circle B, so shade inside A but outside the overlap.

exam.q: A bag contains 3 red counters and 2 blue counters. A counter is taken at random, replaced, and a second counter is taken. Draw a tree diagram to represent this.
model: Start node branching into Red and Blue
Correct second-generation branches from both first nodes
All branches correctly labelled with probabilities or outcomes
exam.tip: Remember 'replaced' means the probabilities stay the same for the second draw.

exam.q: Two tetrahedral (4-sided) dice numbered 1 to 4 are rolled. The scores are added together. Construct a possibility space table to find the number of ways to get a total of 5.
model: Cell values calculated correctly as sums
exam.tip: Carefully check every cell addition before counting your totals.

exam.q: State what the universal set represents in a Venn diagram sorting numbers from 1 to 10.
exam.tip: Keep the definition concise and directly tied to the question context.

exam.q: Explain why listing outcomes systematically is better than random guessing in probability exams.
model: Ensures no outcomes are missed or duplicated
Guarantees full marks for a complete method
exam.tip: Mention organization and completeness to secure both marks.

exam.q: A coin is flipped 3 times. Construct a tree diagram to list all 8 possible sequences of Heads (H) and Tails (T).
model: First split into H and T
Second split into H and T for each branch
Third split into H and T for each second-generation branch
exam.tip: Check 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 to ensure your tree is complete.

worked.q: A cafe sells tea (T) or coffee (C), with a choice of milk (M) or black (B). Construct a systematic tree diagram to list all possible drink combinations and state how many there are.
steps: Step 1: Draw a starting node and draw two branches for the first choice of drink: Tea (T) and Coffee (C).
Step 2: From the end of each drink branch, draw two further branches for milk (M) and black (B).
Step 3: Trace and list all final outcomes: (T,M), (T,B), (C,M), (C,B).
Step 4: Count the final outcomes to get the total.
worked.ans: 4 possible combinations: Tea with milk, Tea black, Coffee with milk, Coffee black.

worked.q: A universal set \u03be contains integers from 1 to 10. Set A is even numbers. Set B is multiples of 3. List the numbers that belong in the intersection A \u2229 B.
steps: Step 1: List the elements of Set A (even numbers from 1 to 10): {2, 4, 6, 8, 10}.
Step 2: List the elements of Set B (multiples of 3 from 1 to 10): {3, 6, 9}.
Step 3: Find the numbers that appear in both lists (the intersection).
Step 4: Identify the common number: 6.

maths_eduqas_f.4.1.summary: These revision notes explore the foundational principles of randomness, fairness, and equally likely outcomes as specified in the Eduqas GCSE Mathematics framework. Students will learn how to identify fair situations, use theoretical probability to predict future results, and distinguish between subjective guesses and mathematical certainty. Mastering these concepts ensures a rock-solid grasp of how probability governs both single events and repeated trials in a controlled environment.

core.p: Randomness describes a situation where individual outcomes cannot be predicted with absolute certainty beforehand, yet each possible outcome has a distinct chance of occurring. In GCSE mathematics, we assume standard items like dice, coins, and spinners behave randomly unless proven biased. Recognizing the true nature of random processes allows us to apply mathematical rules without falling into the trap of looking for false patterns.
bullets: A random process has outcomes that are completely independent of previous outcomes in standard setups.
Unpredictable individual results contrast with predictable long-term patterns.
Physical randomness requires careful execution, such as thoroughly shuffling cards or rolling a fair die.

callouts.p: An experiment or process where the outcome cannot be predicted with certainty in advance, but the set of all possible outcomes is known.
Never assume a real-world object is fair unless the question explicitly states it is fair or unbiased.

core.p: A game, trial, or object is described as fair if every participant or potential outcome has an equal and unbiased opportunity to occur. Fairness eliminates any systemic advantage towards one specific result over another. When examining mathematical scenarios, verifying fairness lets us assign equal numerical probabilities to each outcome in the sample space.
bullets: Fair coins give equal weight to heads and tails.
Fair spinners have sectors of identical area and equal friction.
Biased objects breach the fundamental assumption of equal likelihood.

callouts.p: When outcomes have the exact same chance of occurring, they are termed equally likely.
Confusing a game being fair with the idea that everyone must win an equal number of times in the short term.

core.p: When all individual outcomes in a sample space possess the exact same chance of happening, calculating theoretical probability becomes a simple fraction. The denominator is the total number of possible outcomes, and the numerator is the number of successful outcomes. Understanding this symmetry is essential for accurate predictions.
bullets: Total probability of all outcomes combined must always equal 1.
Every single outcome has a probability of 1 divided by the total number of outcomes.
Symmetry in physical objects guarantees equal likelihood.

callouts.p: The complete, exhaustive list of all possible distinct outcomes of a random trial.
Always ensure your probability fractions are fully simplified unless the question specifies otherwise.

core.p: We use theoretical probability to predict what should happen over a series of trials or on a single trial. While we cannot predict the exact result of one specific flip of a coin, prediction models tell us what proportion of results we expect over hundreds of trials. This bridges the gap between single-event calculation and expected frequency.
bullets: Prediction is based on mathematical expectation, not certainty.
Formula: Expected frequency = Probability of event multiplied by Total number of trials.
Greater number of trials aligns closer to theoretical predictions.

callouts.p: The long-term average outcome calculated by multiplying the probability by the number of trials.
Believing a coin is 'due' to land on tails because it landed on heads five times in a row.

core.p: Spinners are classic mathematical tools used to test understanding of area and equal likelihood. If a spinner is divided into unequal sectors, the outcomes are not equally likely, and probabilities must be calculated using the relative areas of each sector. If sectors are identical, each sector has an equal fraction of the whole circle.
bullets: Check if sector angles or areas are equal before assuming equal likelihood.
Total angle of a spinner equals 360 degrees.
Probability of landing on a specific sector equals sector angle divided by 360.

callouts.p: The likelihood of a spinner stopping on a specific region based on its proportional area or angle.
Sum all given sector angles in a spinner problem to ensure they total 360 degrees.

core.p: A standard six-sided die is the cornerstone of probability questions. Each face contains numbers from 1 to 6. Assuming a fair die, each number has a probability of 1 over 6. Questions often combine numbers into subsets such as primes, squares, or multiples, requiring students to isolate successful outcomes accurately.
bullets: Prime numbers on a standard die: 2, 3, 5.
Square numbers on a standard die: 1, 4.
Even numbers on a standard die: 2, 4, 6.

callouts.p: The set {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} represents all possible outcomes of rolling a standard fair die.
Remember that 1 is not a prime number when counting successful outcomes for prime number questions.

core.p: Exam questions often present a game involving two players and ask whether the game is fair. To prove fairness, calculate the exact probability of each player winning. If both probabilities are identical, the game is fair. If the probabilities differ, explain which player has an advantage and why.
bullets: Calculate Player A winning probability.
Calculate Player B winning probability.
Compare fractions: equal means fair, unequal means unfair.

callouts.p: A game where every player has an identical mathematical probability of winning.
Always state both probabilities clearly before concluding whether a game is fair or unfair.

core.p: Theoretical prediction tells us what should happen in a perfect mathematical world, whereas experimental results show what actually happens in practice. When predicting outcomes for large trials, use the theoretical probability multiplied by the number of trials to find the most likely expected outcome.
bullets: Theoretical probability is calculated without doing the experiment.
Experimental probability is derived from actual trial data.
Discrepancies shrink as sample size grows larger.

callouts.p: As an experiment is repeated more times, the experimental relative frequency approaches the theoretical probability.
If an expected value results in a decimal, give the exact decimal or round sensibly to an integer in context.

core.p: An object is biased if its outcomes do not match the theoretical expectations over a large number of trials. Questions may provide relative frequencies from 200 coin flips and ask whether the coin is likely to be fair. Students must use logical reasoning based on deviation from expected values.
bullets: Look for significant divergence from expected frequencies.
Small sample sizes can show large variation by chance alone.
Always justify conclusions using numbers from the prompt.

callouts.p: A systematic distortion of results that favors one or more outcomes over others.
Do not declare an object biased based on a tiny sample of 5 or 10 trials.

core.p: Probabilities are always expressed on a scale from 0 to 1, or 0% to 100%, or as fractions between 0 and 1. An outcome with a probability of 0 is impossible, while an outcome with a probability of 1 is certain. Predicting outcomes requires placing them correctly on this mathematical continuum.
bullets: 0 means impossible.
0.5 means an even chance.
1 means certain.

callouts.p: No probability can ever be less than 0 or greater than 1, and negative probabilities do not exist.
Fractions, decimals, and percentages are all acceptable unless a specific format is requested.

core.p: Higher-level foundation questions may ask students to design a fair spinner, bag of counters, or ticket draw based on given conditions. This requires dividing items into equal proportions or assigning equal angles to sectors so that every outcome has the exact same chance of being selected.
bullets: Calculate the number of equal parts needed from the denominator.
Ensure total angles sum to 360 degrees for spinners.
Verify equal quantities for colored counters in a bag.

callouts.p: The requirement to create a random apparatus that satisfies specific fairness criteria.
When sketching a spinner, use a protractor mindset to divide angles evenly.

core.p: Everyday language uses terms like 'likely', 'unlikely', 'evens', and 'impossible'. GCSE mathematics requires translating these descriptive phrases into precise numerical values or fractions. Being able to interpret and write these statements ensures clarity in communication.
bullets: 'Even chance' corresponds to 0.5 or 1/2.
'Unlikely' corresponds to a value strictly between 0 and 0.5.
'Likely' corresponds to a value strictly between 0.5 and 1.

callouts.p: Learn standard descriptive probability terms and their corresponding fractional boundaries.
Avoid using casual words like 'maybe' in exams; use precise mathematical terminology.

analogy.p: Imagine a standard fair die as a perfectly balanced cube where every face has an equal footprint and weight: each number has an exact 1 in 6 chance of landing face up. This is like a perfectly fair game of chance. If someone glues a heavy lead weight inside the die beneath the face showing 6, the center of mass shifts. The die now lands on 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 much more often, making the outcomes no longer equally likely. In exams, spotting fairness means checking if the balance is maintained, while predicting outcomes relies on assuming the ideal, unbiased state unless told otherwise.

terms.d: A systematic tendency to favor certain outcomes over others in a random trial.
Outcomes that have the exact same theoretical chance of occurring.
The predicted number of times a specific outcome will occur in a given number of trials.
A game where all participants have an equal probability of winning.
An event with a probability of 0.
Events where the outcome of one does not affect the probability of the other.
The principle that experimental probability gets closer to theoretical probability as sample size increases.
A possible result of a trial or experiment.
A numerical measure of the likelihood that an event will occur, ranging from 0 to 1.
A process where individual outcomes are uncertain, but long-term frequencies follow mathematical laws.
The complete set of all possible outcomes of an experiment.
The likelihood of an event happening based on mathematical reasoning and symmetry.
A single performance of a random experiment or procedure.
Not showing any unfair preference; equally balanced.
An event with a probability of 1.

mistakes.w: Saying a coin will definitely land on heads after five tails because it has to even out.
mistakes.r: Coin tosses are independent; the coin has no memory of past flips.

mistakes.w: Writing probability as 1 out of 6 in words.
mistakes.r: Always write probability as a fraction (1/6), decimal, or percentage.

mistakes.w: Assuming a spinner with different sized sections is fair.
mistakes.r: Fairness requires sectors to have identical areas and angles.

mistakes.w: Writing a probability greater than 1, such as 5/4.
mistakes.r: Probabilities must always be between 0 and 1 inclusive.

mistakes.w: Confusing expected frequency with actual experimental results.
mistakes.r: Expected frequency is a theoretical prediction, not a guarantee of what will happen in a small sample.

mistakes.w: Stating that 1 is a prime number when analyzing a die.
mistakes.r: 1 is not a prime number; prime numbers start at 2.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to simplify probability fractions.
mistakes.r: Always simplify fractions to their lowest terms unless instructed otherwise.

exam.q: A fair six-sided die is rolled once. Write down the probability that it lands on a number greater than 4.
exam.tip: Remember 'greater than 4' does not include 4 itself.

exam.q: A bag contains 3 red counters, 4 blue counters, and 5 green counters. A counter is chosen at random. Find the probability that it is blue.
exam.tip: Always sum the total number of items first to find the denominator.

exam.q: A spinner has 4 equal sectors colored red, blue, green, and yellow. Tim spins it 200 times. Predict how many times the spinner will land on green.
exam.tip: Use the formula: Probability multiplied by total trials.

exam.q: Explain why a coin that lands on heads 80 times out of 100 flips might be biased.
model: State expected number of heads is 50 out of 100.
Explain that 80 is significantly higher than expected, suggesting bias.
exam.tip: Always compare the actual result with the expected theoretical value.

exam.q: A game uses a fair spinner numbered 1 to 5. Player A wins if the spinner lands on an odd number. Player B wins if it lands on an even number. Is this game fair? Explain your answer.
model: Probabilities are unequal (3/5 vs 2/5), so the game is not fair.
exam.tip: Calculate both players' probabilities explicitly to prove fairness or unfairness.

exam.q: A card is drawn at random from a standard pack of 52 playing cards. What is the probability of selecting a red face card?
model: Identify red face cards: Jack, Queen, King of hearts and diamonds (6 cards).
exam.tip: Face cards are Jack, Queen, King. Red suits are hearts and diamonds.

exam.q: Lucy rolls a biased die 300 times. It lands on a six 90 times. Calculate the experimental probability of rolling a six.
model: Use formula: successful trials divided by total trials.
exam.tip: Experimental probability is based on actual trial data from the question.

exam.q: Design a fair spinner with 8 sectors using three different colors: red, blue, and yellow, such that red is twice as likely as blue, and blue is equally likely as yellow.
model: Let yellow = x, blue = x, red = 2x.
Total sectors: x + x + 2x = 4x = 8, so x = 2.
Yellow = 2 sectors, Blue = 2 sectors, Red = 4 sectors.
Check sectors sum to 8 and ratios match.
exam.tip: Set up an algebraic ratio equation when dividing sectors under conditions.

exam.q: Write down a number that could represent the probability of an impossible event.
exam.tip: Impossible events always have a probability of exactly 0.

exam.q: A box contains cards labeled with integers from 1 to 20. One card is drawn at random. Find the probability that the number is a multiple of 3.
model: List multiples of 3 up to 20: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 (6 numbers).
exam.tip: List the multiples carefully so you do not miss any boundary values.

worked.q: A bag contains 5 red counters, 3 blue counters, and 2 green counters. A counter is taken out at random, its color is recorded, and it is put back in the bag. This is done 150 times. Calculate the expected number of times a red counter is chosen.
steps: Find the total number of counters in the bag: 5 + 3 + 2 = 10.
Calculate the theoretical probability of choosing a red counter: 5/10 = 1/2 (or 0.5).
Multiply the probability by the total number of trials: (1/2) multiplied by 150 = 75.

worked.q: A fair spinner has 5 equal sections numbered 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Alex plays a game where he spins the spinner 500 times. Work out the expected number of times the spinner will land on a prime number.
steps: Identify prime numbers on the spinner: 2, 3, and 5 (3 prime numbers).
Calculate the theoretical probability of landing on a prime number: 3/5.
Multiply the probability by the total number of spins: (3/5) multiplied by 500.
Compute the final result: 3 multiplied by 100 = 300.

maths_eduqas_f.4.6.summary: Mastering theoretical possibility spaces allows us to systematically list and evaluate every possible outcome when two or more events occur together. By constructing clear grids or tables, we can accurately determine the total number of possible outcomes and count the successful ones to calculate exact theoretical probabilities. These foundational techniques are essential for solving combined probability questions safely without missing any crucial combinations.

core.p: A possibility space is a visual representation of all the possible outcomes of a combined event. When you roll two dice, flip two coins, or spin two spinners, things happen together. Listing everything systematically ensures no outcome is missed.
bullets: Used when two or more independent events happen together.
Helps count both the total number of outcomes and successful outcomes.
Forms the foundation for writing fractions as probabilities.

callouts.p: A complete list or grid showing all possible outcomes of an experiment.

fig.cap: A simple grid layout showing the axes for two independent events like rolling two four-sided dice.

core.p: To build a standard possibility space grid, assign one event to the horizontal axis (columns) and the other event to the vertical axis (rows). Each inner cell represents a single combined outcome written as a coordinate pair.
bullets: Label the rows clearly with the first event's options.
Label the columns clearly with the second event's options.
Fill every interior cell with the corresponding pair.

callouts.p: Always place the first mentioned event on the vertical axis and the second on the horizontal axis to avoid confusion.

core.p: Once the possibility space is complete, finding probabilities is straightforward. Count the total number of cells in the grid, then count how many cells satisfy the given condition.
bullets: Probability = (Number of successful outcomes) / (Total number of possible outcomes).
Always check if your final fraction can be simplified.
Probabilities must always be between 0 and 1 inclusive.

callouts.p: P(event) = Successful Outcomes / Total Outcomes

core.p: Rolling two 6-sided dice creates a grid of 6 rows by 6 columns, resulting in 36 total outcomes. Questions often ask for the probability of getting a specific sum, a double, or a total greater than a certain number.
bullets: Total outcomes = 6 x 6 = 36.
Doubles are outcomes where both numbers match: (1,1), (2,2), ..., (6,6).
Sum of scores means adding the two numbers together in each cell.

callouts.p: Do not confuse 'rolling a total of 8' with 'rolling an 8'. A standard die only goes up to 6, so sums require two dice.

core.p: Spinners can have numbers, colors, or letters. If Spinner A has 3 sections and Spinner B has 4 sections, the possibility space will have 3 rows and 4 columns, giving 12 total outcomes.
bullets: Multiply the number of options on each spinner to find the total outcomes.
Combine spinner results using addition, multiplication, or pairing depending on the question.
Ensure fair spinners are assumed unless stated otherwise.

core.p: Flipping coins creates simple possibility spaces. For two coins, the outcomes are Head-Head, Head-Tail, Tail-Head, and Tail-Tail. This gives 4 total outcomes.
bullets: H represents Heads and T represents Tails.
Order matters unless the question specifies 'one head and one tail regardless of order'.
Three coins yield 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 outcomes.

core.p: Examiners love asking you to perform operations on the two outcomes in your possibility space. You might be asked to find the sum (add them), difference (subtract smaller from larger), or product (multiply them).
bullets: For sums, scan diagonals on a dice grid as they share the same total.
For differences, subtract the smaller coordinate from the larger one.
For products, multiply the two numbers together.

callouts.p: Sums on a dice grid always form diagonal lines of identical values.

core.p: Two events are mutually exclusive if they cannot happen at the same time. In a possibility space, this means their corresponding cells do not overlap.
bullets: Mutually exclusive outcomes cannot occur simultaneously.
Example: Rolling a sum of 2 and rolling a double 6 on two dice.
Their individual probabilities can be added together.

core.p: Harder exam questions add constraints, such as 'given that the first die is an even number'. This restricts your possibility space, effectively shrinking the total number of possible outcomes.
bullets: Read conditional phrasing carefully.
Cross out rows or columns that do not meet the condition.
Your new denominator is the count of remaining valid cells.

callouts.p: When a condition is given (e.g. 'Given that...'), your denominator changes from the full total to the restricted total.

core.p: When a grid is impractical (such as picking three items or rolling three dice), list the outcomes systematically using an organized tree or structured list.
bullets: Use systematic ordering like alphabetical or numerical sorting.
Check your count against the fundamental counting principle.
Ensure every combination is unique and accounted for.

core.p: Sometimes theoretical possibility spaces are used to predict what will happen in a real experiment carried out many times.
bullets: Multiply the theoretical probability by the number of trials.
Expected frequency = P(event) x Number of trials.
Results are expected values, not guaranteed exact counts.

core.p: Avoid losing easy marks by checking for these common traps before finishing your probability questions.
bullets: Did you simplify your final fraction?
Did you count outcomes twice by misinterpreting order?
Did you use the correct denominator after applying a condition?

callouts.p: Always ensure your probability fraction is between 0 and 1.

analogy.p: Imagine looking at a restaurant menu where you can choose 1 starter from 3 options and 1 main from 4 options. A possibility space is simply the complete grid of every possible 2-course meal you could order. Where the analogy breaks down is that restaurant meals might have sold-out items, whereas mathematical possibility spaces assume every outcome is equally likely and always available.

terms.d: A diagram or list showing all possible outcomes of a combined event.
A single possible result of an experiment or trial.
A collection of one or more outcomes from an experiment.
The likelihood of an event happening based on mathematical reasoning, without experiment.
The set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment.
Events where the outcome of the first does not affect the outcome of the second.
Events that cannot both occur at the same time.
The number of times you expect a specific outcome to occur in a given number of trials.
The result of adding two or more numbers together.
The result of multiplying two or more numbers together.
The result of subtracting one number from another, usually expressed as a positive value.
An outcome in dice rolling where both dice land on the same number.
A single performance of a random experiment or procedure.
A numerical quantity that is not a whole number, used to express probability.

mistakes.w: Adding the probabilities of dependent events incorrectly or leaving fractions unsimplified like 6/36.
mistakes.r: Simplify all fractions to their lowest terms (e.g., 1/6).

mistakes.w: Listing (3,4) and (4,3) as the same outcome when rolling two dice.
mistakes.r: Recognise that two distinct dice mean order matters; (3,4) and (4,3) are separate outcomes.

mistakes.w: Writing probabilities as ratios like 3:36 instead of fractions or decimals.
mistakes.r: Always write probabilities as fractions, decimals, or percentages, never ratios.

mistakes.w: Using 36 as the denominator when a condition has restricted the sample space.
mistakes.r: Adjust the denominator to match only the remaining valid outcomes after applying the condition.

mistakes.w: Confusing the sum of two dice with the product of two dice.
mistakes.r: Carefully check whether the question asks you to add (+) or multiply (x) the outcomes.

mistakes.w: Stating a probability is greater than 1 (e.g., 5/4).
mistakes.r: Remember that probabilities can never exceed 1 or 100%.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to include all combinations in a possibility grid.
mistakes.r: Systematically fill every cell in the grid to ensure complete coverage.

exam.q: Two fair 6-sided dice are rolled. Complete a possibility space grid to show all 36 outcomes.
model: Grid drawn with axes 1 to 6 for both dice.
All 36 coordinate pairs correctly filled in.
exam.tip: Ensure your grid is neat and all 36 cells are clearly visible.

exam.q: Two fair 6-sided dice are rolled. Find the probability that the sum of the numbers is 8.
exam.tip: Look along the diagonal for sum 8.

exam.q: A spinner with sections 1, 2, 3 is spun twice. Find the probability that the two numbers multiplied together give an even number.
exam.tip: Multiply each row and column entry before counting.

exam.q: A coin is flipped and a 4-sided die is rolled. Find the probability of getting a Head and an odd number.
exam.tip: Always simplify your fraction.

exam.q: Two fair 6-sided dice are rolled. Given that the first die shows a 5, find the probability that the sum is greater than 8.
model: Restrict sample space to row where first die is 5 (6 outcomes).
exam.tip: Read 'given that' to restrict your denominator.

exam.q: Two fair tetrahedral (4-sided numbered 1 to 4) dice are rolled. Find the probability of getting a double.
exam.tip: Count matching pairs along the main diagonal.

exam.q: Three fair coins are flipped. List the sample space and find the probability of getting at least two heads.
model: List all 8 outcomes (HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT).
Identify outcomes with at least two heads: HHH, HHT, HTH, THH (4 outcomes).
exam.tip: Systematically list H and T combinations.

exam.q: A bag contains 3 counters: Red, Blue, Green. Two counters are picked with replacement. Find the probability both are the same color.
exam.tip: With replacement means the options do not change for the second pick.

exam.q: Two dice are rolled. Find the probability that the difference between the two numbers is 2.
exam.tip: Difference means subtract the smaller from the larger.

exam.q: Explain why the probability of rolling a total of 13 with two standard 6-sided dice is 0.
model: The maximum possible total on two 6-sided dice is 6 + 6 = 12, so a total of 13 is impossible.
exam.tip: Keep explanation concise and mathematically sound.

worked.q: Two fair 6-sided dice are rolled. Find the probability that the sum of the two numbers is a prime number.
steps: Step 1: Recognize that the total number of outcomes for two 6-sided dice is 6 x 6 = 36.
Step 2: Identify prime numbers possible as sums of two dice (primes between 2 and 12 are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11).
Step 4: Add successful outcomes together: 1 + 2 + 4 + 6 + 2 = 15.
Step 5: Write the probability fraction 15/36 and simplify by dividing numerator and denominator by 3 to get 5/12.

worked.q: A red spinner has numbers 1 and 2. A blue spinner has numbers 1, 2, and 3. Both spinners are spun. Find the probability that the sum of the two spinner numbers is greater than 3.
steps: Step 1: Construct a possibility grid with Red spinner (1, 2) on rows and Blue spinner (1, 2, 3) on columns.
Step 2: Calculate total outcomes = 2 x 3 = 6 possible cells: (1,1), (1,2), (1,3), (2,1), (2,2), (2,3).
Step 4: Identify sums greater than 3: (1,3)=4, (2,2)=4, (2,3)=5. Total successful outcomes = 3.
Step 5: Write probability as 3/6 and simplify to 1/2.

maths_eduqas_f.4.3.summary: These revision notes cover the fundamental probability rule that the sum of probabilities for an exhaustive set of mutually exclusive outcomes always equals exactly 1. You will learn how to identify exhaustive events, find missing probabilities by subtracting known values from 1, and apply this principle across various real-world scenarios in both calculator and non-calculator papers.

core.p: Probability is the numerical measure of how likely an event is to happen. Every probability must lie on a strict scale from 0 to 1 inclusive.
bullets: A probability of 0 means the event is completely impossible.
A probability of 1 means the event is certain to happen.
Probabilities can be written as fractions, decimals, or percentages.
Negative probabilities or probabilities greater than 1 are completely impossible.

callouts.p: 0 <= P(Event) <= 1. Always check that your final probability never exceeds 1 or falls below 0.

fig.cap: The standard probability number line showing impossible, even chance, and certain.

core.p: An exhaustive set of outcomes means a list of all possible things that can happen when an experiment is performed. Nothing else is left out.
bullets: If you roll a standard 6-sided die, the exhaustive outcomes are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6.
If you look at the weather tomorrow, an exhaustive list might be: Rain, Snow, Sun, Cloud.
If an event has outcomes that do not cover every possibility, the set is not exhaustive.
Exhaustive sets guarantee that at least one of the listed outcomes will definitely occur.

callouts.p: A complete list of all possible outcomes for an event where no other outcome is possible.

core.h: 3. The Core Rule: Sum to One
core.p: When you list every single possible outcome of an event (an exhaustive set), the sum of all their individual probabilities must always equal 1.
bullets: P(Outcome 1) + P(Outcome 2) + ... + P(Outcome n) = 1
This is a fundamental axiom in probability theory.
Examiners frequently test this by giving you all probabilities except one and asking you to find the missing value.
Applies to spinners, dice, coloured counters in a bag, and survey outcomes.

callouts.p: Sum of all outcomes = 1

core.p: Because all probabilities in an exhaustive list add up to 1, you can easily calculate a missing probability if you know all the others.
bullets: Step 1: Add up all the known probabilities given in the question.
Step 2: Subtract this total from 1.
Step 3: The result is the probability of the missing outcome.
Always double-check your addition and subtraction.

callouts.p: Line up decimal points carefully when adding numbers like 0.2, 0.35, and 0.15.

core.p: Probabilities are often given as fractions. To find a missing probability, you must add fractions with a common denominator and subtract from 1 (or 1 written as a fraction).
bullets: Find a common denominator before adding fraction probabilities.
Remember that 1 can be written as n/n (e.g., 5/5 or 8/8).
Simplify your final fraction if the question requires it, though unsimplified fractions usually gain method marks.
Check that the numerator equals the denominator in your final sum check.

callouts.p: Never add denominators together when adding fractions! Only add the numerators.

core.p: Sometimes probabilities are expressed as percentages. An exhaustive set of percentage probabilities must sum to 100%.
bullets: Convert percentages to decimals or fractions if you prefer working with them, or keep them as percentages.
Sum of percentage outcomes = 100%.
Subtract the sum of known percentages from 100% to find the missing percentage.
Remember 100% represents the whole (1).

callouts.p: 100% is identical to a probability of 1.

core.p: Exam questions often present probabilities in a frequency or probability table where one entry is missing or represented by a variable like x.
bullets: Look across the row of probabilities.
Set up an equation equating the sum of all entries to 1.
Solve for the unknown variable if necessary.
Ensure all table entries are valid probabilities between 0 and 1.

core.p: Foundation tier exams occasionally test algebra combined with probability by using algebraic expressions for the probabilities of exhaustive outcomes.
bullets: Sum all the algebraic terms and numbers.
Set the expression equal to 1.
Solve the linear equation to find the value of x.
Substitute x back into the expression if asked for the probability of a specific outcome.

callouts.p: After finding x, substitute it back into every outcome and check that they all sum to exactly 1.

core.p: Events are mutually exclusive if they cannot happen at the same time. An exhaustive set is made of mutually exclusive outcomes.
bullets: Rolling a 2 and rolling a 5 on a single die are mutually exclusive.
For mutually exclusive events, the 'OR' rule applies (you add their individual probabilities).
Because the list is exhaustive, the total 'OR' sum of everything is 1.
Mutually exclusive means zero overlap on a Venn diagram.

callouts.p: Events that cannot occur at the same time in a single trial.

fig.cap: A Venn diagram showing mutually exclusive events inside a universal set summing to 1.

core.p: Examiners design specific traps to catch students who do not fully understand the 'sum to one' rule.
bullets: Trap 1: Assuming outcomes are exhaustive when they are not (e.g., outcomes: Red, Blue. What about Green?).
Trap 2: Forgetting to check if fractions have common denominators before adding.
Trap 3: Leaving a probability answer greater than 1 without realising the error.
Trap 4: Writing probability as a ratio (e.g., 2:3) instead of a fraction, decimal, or percentage.

callouts.p: Probabilities are never written as ratios like 1:4. Always use fractions (1/5), decimals (0.2), or percentages (20%).

analogy.p: Imagine a whole pizza representing a probability of 1. If you slice the pizza into different sized pieces (outcomes), every single slice put back together must make the exact whole pizza. If you know the size of 3 out of 4 slices, you can easily figure out the size of the missing slice by seeing how much space is left in the pizza box. This analogy breaks down because real pizza slices can be eaten or dropped, whereas mathematical probabilities are abstract numbers locked permanently between 0 and 1.

terms.d: A numerical measure between 0 and 1 of the likelihood that an event will occur.
A complete list of all possible outcomes for an experiment where no outcome is omitted.
Events that cannot happen at the same time.
A single performance of a random experiment or procedure.
A possible result of a trial or experiment.
The number of times an outcome occurs divided by the total number of trials.
The expected probability of an event based on mathematical reasoning and equal likelihood.
The complete set of all possible outcomes of an experiment.
The top number in a fraction representing the chosen parts.
The bottom number in a fraction representing the total possible equal parts.
The event that does not happen, where P(not A) = 1 - P(A).
When an experiment or object is not fair, causing certain outcomes to occur more often than others.

mistakes.w: Adding the denominators of fractions when summing probabilities.
mistakes.r: Always find a common denominator before adding fraction numerators.

mistakes.w: Stating that probabilities sum to 100 instead of 1.
mistakes.r: Probabilities are expressed on a 0 to 1 scale (or percentages summing to 100%).

mistakes.w: Writing a probability as a ratio like 3:5.
mistakes.r: Probabilities must be single numbers: fractions, decimals, or percentages.

mistakes.w: Assuming any list of outcomes is exhaustive.
mistakes.r: Check that all possible real-world results are included before applying the sum to 1 rule.

mistakes.w: Writing a probability greater than 1, such as 5/4 or 1.2.
mistakes.r: Probabilities can never exceed 1.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to subtract the total from 1 when finding a missing probability.
mistakes.r: Subtract the sum of known probabilities from 1 to find the missing value.

mistakes.w: Leaving algebraic equations unsolved when finding a missing probability variable.
mistakes.r: Form an equation equal to 1 and solve for x fully.

exam.q: A biased spinner has four sections: A, B, C, and D. The table shows the probabilities of landing on A, B, and C. Work out the probability of landing on D.
exam.tip: Add the given decimals first, then subtract from 1.

exam.q: The probabilities that a biased die lands on 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 are 0.1, 0.2, 0.15, 0.25, and 0.1 respectively. Calculate the probability that it lands on 6.
exam.tip: Ensure all five decimals are added accurately before subtracting from 1.

exam.q: A bag contains red, blue, and green counters. The probability of picking a red counter is 1/4 and the probability of picking a blue counter is 1/2. What is the probability of picking a green counter?
exam.tip: Convert 1/2 to 2/4 so you have a common denominator.

exam.q: In a game, the probability of winning is 0.3 and the probability of drawing is 0.15. If the game cannot end in any other way, find the probability of losing.
exam.tip: The phrasing 'cannot end in any other way' confirms the set of outcomes is exhaustive.

exam.q: A probability table has outcomes X, Y, and Z with probabilities 2x, 3x, and 5x. Find the value of x.
exam.tip: Set the sum of the algebraic terms equal to 1.

exam.q: The probability of rain tomorrow is 3/10 and the probability of snow is 1/5. Assuming no other weather type is possible, calculate the probability of neither rain nor snow.
exam.tip: Convert fractions to a common denominator before adding.

exam.q: A football team can win, draw, or lose a match. The probability they win is 0.45 and the probability they draw is 0.3. Work out the probability they do not win.
model: Probability of not winning includes draw and lose (0.3 + 0.25 = 0.55) or 1 - 0.45
exam.tip: Read carefully: 'not winning' means anything other than a win.

exam.q: Explain why the numbers 0.4, 0.3, and 0.5 cannot represent the complete set of probabilities for an exhaustive list of outcomes.
exam.tip: Exhaustive probabilities must sum to exactly 1.

exam.q: A spinner has 5 equally likely sections numbered 1 to 5. What is the sum of the probabilities of landing on each of the 5 sections?
exam.tip: Any exhaustive set of outcomes always sums to 1.

exam.q: The probability that a bus is late is 2/9, and the probability that it is early is 1/3. If it is either late, early, or on time, find the probability that the bus is on time.
exam.tip: Write 1/3 with denominator 9 to combine easily with 2/9.

worked.q:
A bag contains blue, green, yellow, and white counters. The probabilities of picking each counter are given in the table below. Find the missing probability x.
Blue: 0.2
Green: 0.35
Yellow: 0.1
White: x
steps: Step 1: Identify that the set of counters is exhaustive, so all probabilities must sum to 1.
Step 2: Add the known probabilities together: 0.2 + 0.35 + 0.1 = 0.65.
Step 3: Subtract this sum from 1: 1 - 0.65 = 0.35.

worked.q: A biased coin is tossed. The probability of getting a Head is 5/8. What is the probability of getting a Tails?
steps: Step 1: Recognise that Head and Tails form an exhaustive set of outcomes for a single coin toss.
Step 2: State the rule: P(Head) + P(Tails) = 1.
Step 3: Substitute the known value: 5/8 + P(Tails) = 1.
Step 4: Subtract 5/8 from 1 (written as 8/8): 8/8 - 5/8 = 3/8.

maths_eduqas_f.4.4.summary: These revision notes explore how empirical unbiased samples tend towards theoretical probability as sample size increases, a core concept in Eduqas GCSE Foundation probability. We cover relative frequency, experimental trials, the Law of Large Numbers, and how to analyze data tables to evaluate bias and fairness. Mastering these concepts ensures full marks on experimental probability questions in both non-calculator and calculator papers.

core.p: In probability, we study two fundamentally different ways to find the chance of an event occurring: looking at the math beforehand, or running trials in the real world.
bullets: Theoretical probability is calculated mathematically using equally likely outcomes without doing any experiments.
Experimental (empirical) probability is calculated from the results of actual physical trials or real-world observations.
Theoretical formula: P(event) = (Number of successful outcomes) / (Total number of possible equally likely outcomes).
Experimental formula: Relative Frequency = (Number of times an event occurs) / (Total number of trials carried out).

callouts.p: A probability based on frequency data collected from actual experiments or surveys, also known as relative frequency.

core.p: For experimental results to be meaningful and comparable to theoretical expectations, the sample must be truly unbiased and representative.
bullets: An unbiased sample means every trial has an equal opportunity to produce any of the valid outcomes without unfair favoritism.
A biased coin might be weighted on one side, making experimental results permanently skewed away from theory.
Unbiased data collection requires random selection and identical conditions for every single test or trial.
If a die has an indentation or uneven weight, it is biased and its empirical data will never match the theoretical expectation of 1/6.

callouts.p: Never assume an object is unbiased unless stated in the question or proven by large sample data.

core.h: 3. The Effect of Increasing Sample Size
core.p: The heart of this specification point is the relationship between how many times you run an experiment and how close your results get to the truth.
bullets: Small sample sizes produce wild, unreliable fluctuations and high variability.
As the sample size increases, the relative frequency settles down and stabilizes.
Larger samples smooth out random chance anomalies and luck.
An experiment with 10 coin flips might give 80% heads, but 10,000 flips will get extremely close to 50%.

callouts.p: Empirical unbiased samples tend towards theoretical probability as the sample size increases.

fig.cap: Figure 1: Relative frequency converging towards the theoretical probability of 0.5 as sample size increases from 10 to 1000.

core.p: Examiners frequently test your ability to read trial data tables and calculate relative frequencies across different numbers of trials.
bullets: Tables typically show outcomes, tally marks or frequencies, and running totals.
Always check the column headers to ensure you are dividing the frequency of a specific outcome by the cumulative total trials.
Be prepared to calculate relative frequency as a fraction, decimal, or percentage depending on exam wording.
Look for columns showing cumulative totals to evaluate how relative frequency changes as trials accumulate.

callouts.p: Decimals between 0 and 1 are usually the easiest format to compare against theoretical probabilities like 1/6 = 0.166...

core.p: In probability theory, the principle that describes this convergence behavior is formally known as the Law of Large Numbers.
bullets: States that as a sample size grows, its mean gets closer to the expected value of the whole population.
Explains why casinos and insurance companies always make money over millions of customers despite individual random losses.
Guarantees predictability in the long run even when individual events are completely unpredictable.
Forms the scientific bridge between theoretical math models and messy physical reality.

callouts.p: A theorem stating that the relative frequency obtained from a large number of trials tends to approach the theoretical probability.

core.h: 6. Identifying Bias from Small vs Large Samples
core.p: Exam questions often present two sets of data: a small sample and a large sample, asking you to explain which one is more reliable.
bullets: Small samples are heavily distorted by chance variation and luck.
A large sample provides overwhelming evidence of the true underlying probability or bias.
If a coin flipped 20 times gives 15 heads, it could easily be a normal unbiased coin due to chance.
If a coin flipped 10,000 times gives 7,500 heads, it is definitely biased because large samples do not fluctuate that far from 0.5 by pure chance.

callouts.p: Never conclude a dice or coin is biased based on fewer than 30 trials; the sample size is simply too small.

core.p: You can use experimental relative frequency or theoretical probability to predict future outcomes in large trials.
bullets: Formula: Estimated number of successes = (Probability) x (Total number of planned trials).
If the relative frequency of rolling a 3 is 0.18 over 500 rolls, estimate how many times a 3 appears in 2000 rolls by scaling up.
Calculation: 0.18 x 2000 = 360 expected times.
Always state clearly whether you are using theoretical probability or experimental relative frequency for your estimate.

callouts.p: Multiply the probability by the new total number of trials directly.

core.p: Exam tasks often ask you to assess whether a game or spinner is fair using experimental data.
bullets: A fair spinner with 4 equal sections has a theoretical probability of 0.25 for each color.
Compare each experimental relative frequency to the expected theoretical probability of 0.25.
If all experimental values are reasonably close in a large sample, the game is fair.
If one outcome dominates persistently across a large sample, the game is unfair (biased).

callouts.p: Look for closeness between relative frequency and theoretical probability in large sample tables.

fig.cap: Figure 2: Comparing experimental relative frequencies of a 4-section spinner with the theoretical fair probability line at 0.25.

core.p: Examiners love asking written questions about how to improve experimental probability investigations.
bullets: Increase the number of trials (roll more times, flip more times).
Ensure the equipment used (coins, dice, spinners) is tested for unbiased construction.
Combine results from multiple independent groups to pool data into a much larger sample size.
Eliminate human error in recording and tallying outcomes.

callouts.p: The quality of experimental results being trustworthy and consistent, achieved primarily through large sample sizes.

core.p: Visualizing relative frequency on a line graph demonstrates the convergence property instantly.
bullets: The x-axis represents the number of trials; the y-axis represents relative frequency (from 0 to 1).
At the start (low trial count), the line swings up and down dramatically.
As trials increase towards the right of the graph, the line flattens out horizontally close to the theoretical probability value.
Always identify the horizontal asymptote as representing the true theoretical probability.

callouts.p: When asked 'Which estimate is best?', always pick the one corresponding to the largest number of trials.

analogy.t: The Weather Forecast vs Daily Weather
analogy.p: Imagine trying to predict whether it will rain on a specific Tuesday next month (small sample / individual trial)—it is unpredictable and volatile. However, if you look at climate data over 50 years of Julys (large sample), the overall average rainfall percentage becomes extremely stable and predictable. Where the analogy breaks down: climate patterns can actually change over decades due to global shifts, whereas mathematical probability constants like coin flip odds never change.

terms.d: The mathematical likelihood of an event occurring, calculated without experiments using equally likely outcomes.
The likelihood of an event occurring based on actual trial data, expressed as a relative frequency.
The ratio of the number of times an event occurs to the total number of trials performed.
The mathematical principle stating that experimental relative frequency approaches theoretical probability as sample size increases.
A data collection sample where every outcome has a fair, equal chance of occurring without systematic favoritism.
Unfairly weighted or skewed towards favoring certain outcomes over others.
The total number of trials, observations, or tests conducted in an experiment.
The process where experimental relative frequency values settle closer and closer to a single fixed theoretical value.
The predicted number of times an event should occur in a given number of trials based on probability.
A single performance of an experiment or random test, such as rolling a die or flipping a coin.
The exact count of how many times a particular outcome occurs in an experiment.
The degree to which experimental data can be trusted as accurate, heavily dependent on large trial counts.

mistakes.w: Saying that 10 coin flips guaranteeing 5 heads proves the law of large numbers.
mistakes.r: Small samples fluctuate wildly; 10 flips is far too small to demonstrate reliable convergence.

mistakes.w: Adding the frequencies from different trial sizes together into a single sum without dividing by total trials.
mistakes.r: Always calculate relative frequency as frequency divided by the corresponding total trials for that experiment.

mistakes.w: Believing a coin 'remembers' previous flips (Gambler's Fallacy).
mistakes.r: Each trial is independent; past coin flips do not influence future coin flips.

mistakes.w: Stating that experimental probability always equals theoretical probability exactly.
mistakes.r: Experimental probability only tends towards or approximates theoretical probability as sample size increases.

mistakes.w: Choosing a small sample result as the 'best estimate' because it was the first trial.
mistakes.r: The best estimate is always derived from the largest sample size available.

mistakes.w: Writing relative frequency as a ratio like 3:7 instead of a fraction, decimal, or percentage.
mistakes.r: Relative frequency must be expressed as a fraction, decimal, or percentage between 0 and 1.

mistakes.w: Assuming a spinner is fair immediately without checking frequency data.
mistakes.r: Fairness must be evaluated by comparing experimental frequencies to expected theoretical values.

exam.q: A biased spinner has four sections: A, B, C, and D. Sarah spins it 500 times. Section A occurs 200 times. Work out the relative frequency of spinning A.
exam.tip: Put the frequency of the successful outcome over the total number of trials.

exam.q: Explain why 500 spins gives a more reliable estimate of probability than 5 spins.
model: Larger sample sizes reduce the impact of random chance and experimental variation / tend closer to theoretical probability.
exam.tip: Use key phrases like 'larger sample size' and 'reduces chance variation'.

exam.q: Liam rolls a biased die 50 times and gets a six 15 times. Estimate the probability of rolling a six based on Liam's results.
exam.tip: Experimental probability uses the trials performed, not the theoretical 1/6.

exam.q: A coin is flipped 1000 times and lands on heads 512 times. Does this prove the coin is biased? Explain your answer.
model: No, it does not prove bias.
512 out of 1000 is very close to 500 (0.5), which is expected due to natural sample variation.
exam.tip: Large samples allow small deviations from 0.5 simply due to random chance.

exam.q: The relative frequency of scoring a goal for a hockey player is 0.35 over 200 shots. Estimate how many goals she will score in 1000 shots.
exam.tip: Multiply the relative frequency by the new number of total trials.

exam.q: State what happens to the relative frequency of an event as the number of unbiased trials increases.
model: It tends towards / gets closer to the theoretical probability.
exam.tip: Learn this exact specification phrasing for full marks.

exam.q: A bag contains coloured counters. Priya takes a counter, notes the colour, and replaces it. Table: 50 trials = 12 reds; 500 trials = 135 reds. Which relative frequency is the better estimate for picking a red counter? Give a reason.
model: Because a larger sample size is more reliable / closer to the true probability.
exam.tip: Always select the larger sample size and justify with sample size reasoning.

exam.q: Complete the sentence: As the sample size increases, empirical unbiased samples tend towards __________ probability.
exam.tip: Fill-in-the-blank specification terminology.

exam.q: A spinner is spun 200 times. It lands on blue 80 times. Calculate the relative frequency of blue as a decimal.
exam.tip: Simplify 80/200 to 8/20 then 4/10 = 0.4.

exam.q: Give one reason why an experimental probability might differ from a theoretical probability when only 10 trials are carried out.
model: Due to chance variation / small sample size / fluke results.
exam.tip: Mention small sample size or random variation.

worked.q:
A football team records their penalty shootout results across different numbers of attempts. 
- After 50 attempts: 32 successful. 
- After 500 attempts: 340 successful. 
(a) Calculate the relative frequency of success for 50 attempts and 500 attempts. 
(b) Explain which figure gives a better estimate of the true probability of scoring a penalty and why.
steps: (a) For 50 attempts: 32 / 50 = 0.64 (or 64%).
(b) The 500 attempts figure is a better estimate.
(b) Reason: Larger sample sizes reduce the effect of random variation and tend closer to the true theoretical probability.
worked.ans: (a) 0.64 and 0.68. (b) 500 attempts because larger sample sizes are more reliable.

worked.q:
A student tests a six-sided die by rolling it 600 times. The number 5 appears 120 times. 
(a) What is the theoretical probability of rolling a 5 on a fair die? 
(b) What is the experimental relative frequency of rolling a 5 in this experiment? 
(c) Based on the 600 rolls, does the die appear to be fair or biased towards rolling a 5? Explain.
steps: (a) Theoretical probability = 1/6 (approx 0.167).
(b) Experimental relative frequency = 120 / 600 = 1/5 = 0.20.
(c) Compare 0.20 to 0.167. 0.20 is higher than expected.
(c) With a large sample of 600 rolls, a relative frequency of 0.20 suggests the die is biased towards rolling a 5.
worked.ans: (a) 1/6 (0.167). (b) 0.20. (c) Biased towards 5, because 0.20 is noticeably higher than 1/6 in a large sample.

maths_eduqas_f.4.7.summary: Mastering tree diagrams is essential for calculating probabilities of combined events at Foundation tier. Independent events have no effect on each other, meaning probabilities stay constant across trials, while dependent events change based on prior outcomes. By multiplying along branches and adding across paths, students can systematically solve complex two-stage probability problems.

core.h: 1. Introduction to Combined Events and Tree Diagrams
core.p: Combined events involve two or more sequential or simultaneous trials, such as rolling a die twice or taking two counters from a bag. A tree diagram is a visual tool that maps out all possible outcomes and their respective probabilities across successive stages. Every branch represents a specific outcome, and the structure ensures no path is missed.
bullets: Shows the sequence of two or more independent or dependent events
Consists of main branches for the first event and sub-branches for the second event
Helps organise outcomes systematically to calculate combined probabilities
Crucial for both non-calculator and calculator papers in Eduqas GCSE

callouts.p: A diagram used to show the probabilities of combined events, consisting of branches labelled with probabilities.

fig.cap: Basic tree diagram structure showing first and second events

core.h: 2. The Golden Rule: Probabilities Add to 1
core.p: At any given point on a tree diagram where branches split from a single node, the sum of all probabilities must equal exactly 1. This rule applies to every single set of branching paths and acts as a built-in check for your working. If your branch probabilities do not sum to 1, an error has been made.
bullets: Every set of branching outcomes from a single point sums to 1
Applies to both first-stage and second-stage branches
If one probability is known, the other can be found by subtracting from 1
Essential for verifying fractions or decimals before multiplying

callouts.p: P(A) + P(not A) = 1 for any single set of branching choices.

core.p: Independent events are those where the outcome of the first event has **no effect** upon the outcome of the second event. Examples include spinning a spinner twice or rolling a standard six-sided die twice. Because the conditions do not change, the probabilities on the second set of branches remain identical to the first set.
bullets: The second event is completely unaffected by the first event
Probabilities on the second set of branches stay the same
Example: replacing a counter after taking it out (replacement)
Example: tossing a fair coin multiple times

core.p: Dependent events occur when the outcome of the first event **does affect** the probability of the second event. The classic GCSE scenario is selecting items from a bag **without replacement**. When a counter or marble is removed and not put back, the total number of items decreases by 1, and the number of specific items may also decrease by 1.
bullets: The outcome of the first event changes the denominator (total)
Numerator may also decrease if a matching item was removed
Example: taking two counters from a bag without replacement
Probabilities on second-stage branches must be carefully recalculated

callouts.p: Events where the outcome of the first event affects the probability of the second event.
Always remember to reduce both the numerator and the denominator for the second set of branches if an item is not replaced.

core.p: To find the probability of a combined sequence of events occurring together (along a specific path), you must **multiply** the probabilities along those branches. This is known as the multiplicative rule or the AND rule in probability. For example, the probability of getting Red AND Red is P(Red) multiplied by P(Red given Red).
bullets: Multiply probabilities along the branches (left to right)
P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B given A)
Fractions: multiply numerators together and denominators together
Decimals: use standard decimal multiplication methods

callouts.p: Multiply probabilities along the branches for combined sequential events.

core.p: When a question asks for an outcome that can happen in **more than one way** (e.g., 'one red and one blue' can be Red then Blue OR Blue then Red), you calculate the probability of each path separately and then **add** those probabilities together. This is the additive rule or the OR rule.
bullets: Calculate the final probability for each valid path by multiplying
Add the outcomes of the separate paths together
P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) for mutually exclusive paths
Ensure fractions share a common denominator before adding if non-calculator

callouts.p: Add the probabilities of different mutually exclusive paths that satisfy the required outcome.

core.p: To construct an accurate tree diagram in an exam, follow a clear method. First, identify all possible outcomes for the first event and draw branches with their probabilities. Next, for each first-stage branch, draw the second-stage branches reflecting whether the events are independent or dependent. Finally, label all branches clearly with fractions or decimals.
bullets: Read the question carefully to check for replacement ('with' or 'without')
Draw neat lines using a ruler and label all nodes clearly
Write fraction probabilities in their simplest form where appropriate
Check that branches originating from the same point add up to 1

callouts.p: Keep your tree diagram large and well-spaced so you have plenty of room to write fractions clearly on every branch.

core.p: At the end of every branch path, write the combined outcome (e.g., RR, RB, BR, BB) and calculate its probability. To ensure complete accuracy, you can add up all the final path probabilities on your diagram. They **must sum to exactly 1**. If they do not, an arithmetic or fraction error has occurred in your working.
bullets: List every final combined outcome at the right-hand side of the diagram
Multiply across each path to find the exact final fraction or decimal
Sum all final outcome probabilities to verify they equal 1
Use this check to catch silly mistakes before moving on

callouts.p: The sum of all final path probabilities at the end of a tree diagram is always exactly 1.

core.p: Exam questions may present probabilities as fractions, decimals, or occasionally percentages. Fractions must be multiplied by multiplying numerators and denominators. Decimals can be multiplied using standard methods (ignoring decimal points first, then adjusting). Ensure consistency; do not mix fractions and decimals on the same tree diagram.
bullets: Fractions: multiply tops together, bottoms together (simplify at the end if needed)
Decimals: count total decimal places in the question to check your answer
Percentages: convert to decimals (divide by 100) or fractions before calculating
Never mix representations on the same tree diagram

callouts.p: It is often easier *not* to simplify fractions on intermediate branches, as keeping a common denominator makes adding final paths much easier.

core.p: A common grade 9 style question asks for the probability of getting **'at least one'** of a specific outcome across multiple trials (e.g., 'at least one six in two rolls'). While you could add up all paths containing at least one six, it is much faster and less prone to error to use the **complementary probability** method: 1 minus the probability of getting *none*.
bullets: Identify all paths that contain zero instances of the target outcome
Calculate the probability of that single path (e.g., None AND None)
Subtract that result from 1: P(at least one) = 1 - P(none)
Saves significant time and reduces risk of missing a path

callouts.p: P(at least one) = 1 - P(none)

core.p: In Paper 1 (non-calculator), tree diagram probabilities will usually be simple fractions (e.g., halves, thirds, quarters, fifths) where arithmetic is straightforward. In Paper 2 (calculator), probabilities may be given as decimals or more complex fractions, allowing you to use decimal multiplication and division efficiently.
bullets: Paper 1: leave fractions unsimplified during working to keep common denominators
Paper 2: decimals are fully acceptable; use your calculator carefully
Always write down the full decimal or fraction calculation before evaluating
Check rounding instructions if decimals do not terminate

callouts.p: Always re-enter multiplication of fractions or decimals into your calculator twice to prevent slip-up errors.

core.h: 12. Common Exam Traps and Examiner Expectations
core.p: Examiners frequently penalise students who forget to change denominators in 'without replacement' scenarios, or who add probabilities along branches instead of multiplying them. Always show full working: write down the multiplication expression for the path and the addition expression for combined paths to secure method marks even if arithmetic slips.
bullets: Never add probabilities along a branch (always multiply)
Never multiply probabilities of separate paths when combining (always add)
In dependent events, make sure the second denominator decreases
Always write down your intermediate fraction/decimal products

callouts.p: Examiners award method marks for correct multiplication along branches, even if the final addition has an arithmetic error.

analogy.p: Imagine hiking down a mountain where every path splits into two distinct trails: a left trail and a right trail. If you flip a coin at each junction to decide which way to go, the chance of choosing a specific sequence of turns depends entirely on whether someone is tampering with your map (dependent) or not (independent). To find your final destination hut, you multiply the fraction chance of taking each turn along your specific route. If two different routes lead to the same mountain hut, you add their separate route chances together to find the total probability of ending up there.

mistakes.r: Probabilities along branches must always be multiplied, never added.

mistakes.w: Multiplying probabilities across different paths together
mistakes.r: Probabilities of separate successful paths must be added together, not multiplied.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to decrease the denominator in 'without replacement' questions
mistakes.r: When an item is removed, the total number of items (denominator) decreases by 1 for the next stage.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to decrease the numerator when a specific item is removed
mistakes.r: If a red counter is removed, the number of red counters available for the second draw must also decrease by 1.
